catalog_quote: With the exception of the monosyllabic particles, that are either enclitic or proclitic, each word in Coos has its stress accent, designated by the acute mark (') or by the rising tone rendered here by ^. The former accent is not inseparably associated with any particular syllable of a word. It may, especially in cases of polysyllabic stems, be shifted freely from one syllable to another, although it is very possible that this apparent shifting of accent may be largely due to the rapidity with which the words in question were pronounced by the natives. The circumflex accent appears mostly on the last syllable, and may best be compared with the intonation given to the word so in the English interrogative sentence Is that so ? new_statements.quote: [p. 18] Higher tone, varying from a third to an octave and subject to rhetorical factors, is integral with stress-accent. In Miluk the stressed long vowel usually takes a high-to-level or high-falling tone. In Hanis the stressed element of double length does not always fall in tone but may remain high until completion of the syllable. Short stressed elements take high tone in both dialects. Special tonal indications to distinguish Hanis from Miluk were not made because tonal behavior is regularly as described and contingent upon the primary factor of stress. [p. 16] Prosodic emphasis in Coos is upon a proper weighting of syllables.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog record (classification lexical, from Frachtenberg 1914/1922: each word has a stress accent not tied to a particular syllable, marked by acute or by a 'rising tone' ^). Jacobs confirms the type — a stress-accent language, not a tone language — and adds that the pitch movement Frachtenberg wrote as a second accent mark is a regular, non-distinctive concomitant of stress ('contingent upon the primary factor of stress'), with Hanis/Miluk contour detail and a syllable-weight component. He is silent on where stress falls (no placement rule; calls syllable stress an open problem), so he neither confirms nor disputes the 'free/shifting' placement claim; nothing contradic…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Unclear as to PLACEMENT, not contradictory: Jacobs affirms that Coos (both Hanis and Miluk) has a stress-accent, which he marks on each word in his transcriptions (raised accent after the stressed vowel, e.g. M. hu-'mis, H. kwa'nyau), and states that pitch is not independent: higher tone 'is integral with stress-accent' and 'contingent upon the primary factor of stress' (stressed long vowels high-level or high-falling in Miluk, may stay high through the syllable in Hanis; short stressed vowels high in both). Prosody rests on 'a proper weighting of syllables'; an accented CVC syllable closed by n, m, l is often made heavy by lengthening the sonorant (non-phonemic). He gives NO rule for which syllable carries the stress and explicitly lists 'the problem of syllable stress in both dialects' among the unresolved recording difficulties, deferring a full treatment to a future grammar. Vowels in final unaccented syllables are reduced (a > obscure vowel; i dulled).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress. Related detail only: emphatic/augmentative extra lengthening marked by repeated raised periods (he-'--niye 'long long ago'); heavy accented CVC syllables via sonorant lengthening.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress placement. Dialect difference in the pitch contour of stressed long vowels (Miluk high-to-level or high-falling; Hanis may remain high to the end of the syllable). Monosyllabic particles/proclitics receive 'the weight of a light syllable' in phrase clusters (p. 16).
new_statements.identity_note: Jacobs's texts and phonetics come from a single speaker, Mrs. Annie Miner Peterson (fieldwork 1933-1934), and cover BOTH Coos varieties, Hanis (H.) and Miluk (M.); Glottolog coos1249 is Hanis Coos, with Miluk catalogued separately (milu1241). The stress/tone statement is made for both dialects, with the pitch-contour difference noted; the catalog's Frachtenberg record is based on Hanis.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: verbatim at Frachtenberg 1922 sec. 5 p.309 in both copies we hold (scanned and PDF text, p.23). Deciding source is the language's only reference grammar, and both StressTyp2 (LEX, same page) and WALS cite nothing else for stress, so the record is correctly sourced and the lexical/no-rule reading follows the text (no placement rule; one accent-type minimal pair). sources.note: Secondhand typological coding: Hanis is coded 'No tones' for WALS 13A (three-way scale no tones / simple / complex). The only reference attached to the datapoint is Zenk 1990 (an ethnographic Handbook chapter), so the classification does not visibly rest on Pierce 1971 or Jacobs 1939; it contradicts nothing first-hand but also does not engage Jacobs' remark that higher tone is 'integral with stress-accent' or Frachtenberg's rising 'circumflex' accent.
